source: Gu et al. (2024) LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity
finding: Builds a retrieval pipeline that pulls prior innovations at four generalisation levels (L1-L4), then a two-stage agent combines them. Beats plain direct generation on similarity to the real paper's idea.
numbers: Claude-3.5-Sonnet; 87 papers from OAG-Bench with 3-5 references each. Field similarity (SPECTER cosine) proposed vs baseline: design rationale 0.85 vs 0.78, universal principles 0.83 vs 0.75, key mechanisms 0.87 vs 0.77. Abstract claims 7-10% gain.
limits: Read through a fetched HTML text (first 100k of 207k chars). No human or LLM judge, no ablation, one backbone, one weak baseline. Measures similarity to the published idea, not novelty or value, so it rewards re-deriving known work.
agent_relevance: Closest direct source for O7 as retrieval plus combination. Weak evidence: supports only that retrieved multi-level sources beat no retrieval.

source: Gu et al. (2024) LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity: generalisation-level retrieval design
finding: Key design idea: abstract each source innovation to four levels (problem-specific up to universal principle) and retrieve per level, so the distant match happens at the abstract level, not by surface words.
numbers: Embeddings text-embedding-3-large; one top-ranked innovation kept per level after a similarity filter. Stage 1: component analysis, cross-domain application, building-block assessment. Stage 2: integration into 4 fields.
limits: Level definitions are the authors' own; no test of which level matters. No distance-versus-quality curve.
agent_relevance: Usable pattern for open mode: store a source as (problem, mechanism, principle) and match on principle. Needs our own test of which level to match on.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Blind human study: LLM-agent ideas judged more novel than expert ideas, but weaker on feasibility. Agent: retrieve 10 papers, mass generate, rank.
numbers: Over 100 NLP researchers. Reviews as independent points (Table 7): novelty human 4.84 (n=119 reviews) vs AI 5.64 (n=109) vs AI+human rerank 5.81; excitement 4.55 vs 5.19 vs 5.46; feasibility 6.61 vs 6.34 vs 6.44 (n.s.); effectiveness 5.13 vs 5.47 (n.s.); overall 4.68 vs 4.85 (n.s.) vs 5.34 (p=0.04). 49 ideas per condition.
limits: Novelty judged before any execution. Only NLP prompting topics. Authors say human novelty judgement is hard. Review-level p-values treat reviews as independent.
agent_relevance: Open-mode ideas can read as novel to experts. Do not take that as proof of value; see c05.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?: diversity collapse
finding: Mass generation hits a diversity wall: most generated ideas are near-duplicates.
numbers: 4000 seed ideas per topic; dedup by all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cosine > 0.8 left about 5 percent, around 200 non-duplicates. Prompt appended titles of earlier ideas to avoid repeats and it still plateaued.
limits: One model (Claude-3.5-Sonnet), threshold chosen by manual inspection.
agent_relevance: Supports the rule that many draws from one model are not independent. Open mode needs dedupe and an outside diversity source (retrieved distant concepts), not just more samples.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: When experts actually executed the ideas, the LLM ideas lost their novelty edge.
numbers: 43 experts completed (66 onboarded), 100+ hours each. Idea means (N=19 human, 24 AI ideas): novelty ideation 4.912 human vs 5.778 AI; after execution 4.903 vs 4.729 (n.s.). Pre-to-post gap: novelty human -0.010, AI -1.049 (p=0.025); excitement 0.078 vs -1.760; effectiveness -0.052 vs -1.879; overall -0.628 vs -1.976 (all p<0.05, FDR).
limits: Few ideas, one topic area, executor skill varies. Final human vs AI difference after execution not significant.
agent_relevance: Strongest warning for O7: output that looks novel at idea stage may not survive running. Select by running or checking, never by how novel it reads.

source: Wenger and Kenett (2025) We're Different, We're the Same: Creative Homogeneity Across LLMs
finding: Across 22 LLMs on standard creativity tests, LLM answers are much more similar to each other than human answers are to each other, after controlling for response structure.
numbers: 22 LLMs (Llama 3/3.1, Mistral, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5, Phi-3, Cohere, Jamba and others) vs a human sample; originality by GloVe 840B cosine distance; one-sided Welch t-test, alpha 0.01.
limits: Embedding originality is a proxy; tests are short-form, not combination tasks. Per-test effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Swapping models will not fix lack of diversity. Variety must come from inputs (retrieved concepts, forced distance), not from voting among models.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: On 26K open-ended real queries, one model repeats itself and different models converge on the same outputs.
numbers: Average pairwise similarity among responses to one prompt typically above 0.8 (top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0) vs 0.1-0.2 for random pairs. In 79 percent of cases it stays above 0.8 even at min-p 0.1, temperature 2.0. Cross-model pairs 71-82 percent similar (DeepSeek-V3 and qwen-max 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 and gpt-4o 0.81). 31,250 human annotations, 25 per item.
limits: Embedding-based similarity. Reward models and LLM judges were also miscalibrated on items where human tastes differ.
agent_relevance: Temperature does not buy true variety. LLM judges are weakest exactly where taste differs, matching G5.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024) Divergent Creativity in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: On the Divergent Association Task (name 10 unrelated words, scored by mean semantic distance), GPT-4 beat the human average but top humans stayed ahead. Pure semantic distance, the base skill for far combination.
numbers: 100,000 human responses; GPT-4 significantly above humans, GeminiPro indistinguishable, GPT-4-turbo worse than GPT-4. GPT-4 at temperature 1.5: mean 85.6, above 72 percent of humans (temperatures 0.5, 1.0, 1.5; n=500 each). Strategy suffix 'varying etymology' beat the plain prompt for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; thesaurus beat it for GPT-4 only.
limits: Word-list task, not concept combination. High repetition: 'microscope' in 70 percent of GPT-4 sets, 'ocean' in over 90 percent for GPT-4-turbo. Newer version did not mean higher score.
agent_relevance: Distance can be raised by temperature and a strategy line, but the model repeats itself. Use retrieved or random seed words rather than trusting the model to pick distant items.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Self-generated analogical exemplars (model recalls related problems before solving) beat 0-shot CoT and often match or beat manual few-shot CoT. Analogy used inside a prompt.
numbers: Codeforces Acc@1/Acc@10, GPT-4: 3-shot CoT 16%/30%; self-generated knowledge plus exemplars 19%/37%. GPT-3.5 reaches 15% Acc@1 vs GPT-4 baseline 16%. GSM8K text-davinci-003 roughly 15% (weakest row) to 61% (best row). BIG-Bench word sorting 66.8% (0-shot CoT) to 75.2%. K=5 exemplars for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH and BIG-Bench.
limits: Sources are near (same task type), not distant. PDF table text was jumbled so some values are ranges, not row-exact. Gains for strong models are small.
agent_relevance: Cheap analogue of O7 where the source is the model's own memory. Supports near analogy only; do not cite for distant transfer.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat college students on text matrix, letter-string and verbal analogies, but was clearly worse on story analogies.
numbers: Digit matrices vs N=40 UCLA undergraduates (GPT-3 above average on all problem types; subtype correlation r(30)=0.39, p=0.027). Letter strings N=57: GPT-3 OR=1.76, p=6.3e-5. Story analogies N=54: humans better, OR=0.37, p=0.0003 (15 of 54 chose the analogous story every trial); GPT-4 nearly perfect in a preliminary test.
limits: Zero-shot claim contested, see c12 and c13.
agent_relevance: Models can map structure when the source is shown. The hard part is finding the source, see c14.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models: Gick-Holyoak radiation problem
finding: GPT-3 reproduced the human pattern: used the analogy when handed the analogous story, lost it when two distractor stories were added, recovered it when told to consider the earlier stories.
numbers: Qualitative single test, no counts.
limits: Preliminary, tiny, qualitative.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the schema note that unaided analogy rarely transfers and a mapping step is needed. Selecting from distractors is the bottleneck.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Re-test of Webb's letter-string analogies with permuted or non-letter alphabets: humans stay high, GPT models drop sharply.
numbers: Humans and three GPT models on original and counterfactual alphabets. 38.59 percent of GPT-3.5 errors came from applying an alternate rule (GPT-4 22 percent, GPT-3 5.81 percent). GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 no better than GPT-3 on these.
limits: Letter-string domain only; per-condition accuracies are in figures and were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Do not assume analogy skill survives unfamiliar surface forms. Check mapping on an altered version (G3 mutated-input check).

source: Hodel and West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed replication of Webb on modified letter-string tasks: with a synthetic alphabet GPT-3 collapses on several task types.
numbers: GPT-3 generative accuracy on the synthetic alphabet below 0.1 for extend-sequence, successor/predecessor and fix-alphabetic-sequence; only remove-redundant-letter and sort stay near the original range. Comprehension checks: at least 30 percent of original accuracy on all but one task, so the model did read the change.
limits: Argues the original items may be in training data (ChatGPT could produce letter-string examples; circumstantial). One paper, GPT-3 only.
agent_relevance: Benchmark gains in analogy may be contaminated. Use fresh, altered material in our own checks.

source: AnaloBench (2024) Benchmarking the Abilities of Language Models to Reason about Abstract and Long-context Analogies
finding: Finding the analogous story in a bank is the hard step. Scale helps little for long stories or a large bank. Retrieval of the source, not the mapping, is the weak link.
numbers: 340 human-written analogies. T1 accuracy at 1/10/30 sentences: GPT-4 89.1/66.5/60.7; human 96.0/72.5/73.3; GPT-3.5 65.3/46.4/30.8; Claude 68.2/30.2/25.9; chance 25 percent. Full story bank (T2): GPT-4-Turbo and Claude near a random baseline except 1-sentence GPT-4-Turbo. GPT-4 on Claude-written stories shows negligible drop, so self-preference does not explain it.
limits: Long stories are GPT-4 or Claude expansions of the one-sentence originals. Author names not recorded.
agent_relevance: Predicts that giving the agent a bank of distant sources and expecting it to pick the right one will fail. Retrieval needs code (embeddings, typed fields), not the model's memory.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) AnalogyKB: Unlocking Analogical Reasoning of Language Models with a Million-scale Knowledge Base
finding: Builds a million-scale analogy knowledge base from knowledge graphs; LLMs filter analogies of analogous (not identical) relations. Training on it is claimed to help small LMs on analogy tasks.
numbers: Example in paper: nucleus-electron vs sun-earth; same-relation and analogous-relation types. Benchmark numbers not extracted.
limits: Only abstract and intro read; no numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: A way to get typed source-target pairs offline to feed a mapping step.

source: Krenn et al. (2022) Predicting the Future of AI with AI
finding: Combinational creativity as link prediction: build a concept co-occurrence graph from many AI papers and predict which concept pairs will be combined in a future paper. Hand-built network features beat learned features.
numbers: Task scored by ROC AUC (random 0.5). arXiv AI paper count doubling about every 23 months. Winning AUC not extracted.
limits: A pair being combined later is not a measure of value. High-degree (popular) concepts gain share of edges over time, so the method favours popular pairs.
agent_relevance: An old non-LLM method for choosing which concept pairs to join; a cheap prior on plausible far pairs. Not tested with an LLM agent.

source: Li et al. (2024) Chain of Ideas
finding: Organising retrieved literature as a progression chain gives better LLM ideas than flat paper dumps and is claimed comparable to humans on an Idea Arena protocol.
numbers: Abstract: CoI 'consistently outperforms other methods'; minimum cost $0.50 per candidate idea. Win rates not extracted.
limits: Judging by an LLM arena aligned to human preference; no execution test. Retrieves near literature (one research line), not distant domains.
agent_relevance: Structure of retrieved context matters. Serves as the near-source control for far combination.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Nova: An Iterative Planning and Search Approach to Enhance Novelty and Diversity of LLM Generated Ideas
finding: Iterative planned retrieval (plan what to retrieve, add it, regenerate) raises the count of unique novel ideas and top-rated ideas versus other agents.
numbers: 3.4 times more unique novel ideas than without iterative planning; at least 2.5 times more top-rated ideas than prior agents on 170 seed papers (Swiss Tournament); 619 and 2521 Nova ideas scored 4 and 5. Human check: 10 NLP experts, 20 ideas per topic.
limits: Mostly automatic LLM ratings with a small human panel. Novelty judged by reading, not execution (see c05).
agent_relevance: Numbers for iterated retrieval as a diversity engine. The novelty gain per retrieval round is a quantity our open mode should test.

source: Radensky et al. (2024) Scideator: Human-LLM Scientific Idea Generation Grounded in Research-Paper Facet Recombination
finding: Recombines purpose, mechanism and evaluation facets from papers at set distances (input, near, far, very far) using analogy. Users got more creativity support than with a plain LLM baseline.
numbers: Within-subjects N=22 CS researchers (16 PhD students). Creativity Support Index median 70.5 vs 61.0, Wilcoxon p<.01; biggest gains in exploration and expressiveness. Participants used input and near facets far more than far facets, mainly for seeming irrelevant; 4 found far ones useful for discovery. 12 facet pairs per run (3 distances x 4).
limits: Self-rated support, not idea quality. Version v7 (May 2026); earlier versions may differ. First-author name not verified from the page.
agent_relevance: When free to choose, people avoid far sources. Far sources must be forced by the program; relevance filtering decides how far is usable.

source: Ma et al. (2023) Conceptual Design Generation Using Large Language Models
finding: LLM design solutions were compared with crowdsourced ones; few-shot examples pulled outputs toward the crowd solutions, i.e. less novel.
numbers: Authors state few-shot prompting yields solutions more similar to crowdsourced ones; expert ratings of novelty, feasibility and usefulness used. Numbers not extracted.
limits: Design domain, small experiment.
agent_relevance: Examples in the prompt act as anchors. Show sources only after the first unprimed draw (matches fixation work).

source: Gu et al. (2024) framing and reading list
finding: Theory frame is Boden (2004): combinatorial, exploratory, transformational creativity, plus the Four P's; the method sits in the Process view with retrieval giving cross-domain concepts.
numbers: Cited LLM ideation works: Si 2409.04109, Kumar 2409.06185, SciMON 2305.14259, Qi 2311.05965, ResearchAgent 2404.07738, AI Scientist 2408.06292.
limits: Citation list taken from a fetched page summary; only 2409.04109 was verified.

source: Synthesis across opened sources: distance and combination
finding: Across Scideator (c19), AnaloBench (c14), Webb (c10, c11) and Si (c03, c05): far sources are used less, found less, and ideas that look novel were less runnable. No opened study measured a clean distance-versus-value curve for LLM combination.
numbers: Anchors: Scideator far facets used less than near; AnaloBench bank retrieval near random for long stories; Si 2025 AI novelty drop -1.049 after execution.
limits: My synthesis, not a measured result. SUBFIELDS open question 3 stays unanswered.
agent_relevance: Plan our own test: grounded vs ungrounded draws at three source distances, scored by running or blind raters.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?: LLM self-evaluation and ranking
finding: Paper reports LLM self-evaluation of ideas failed and LLMs are not reliable evaluators; human reranking raised the overall score.
numbers: AI+human rerank overall 5.34 vs human ideas 4.68 (p=0.04); LLM-only ranked AI ideas overall 4.85 (n.s.).
limits: Ranker accuracy figures not extracted.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: the model should not pick the best combination. Selection needs a blind or outside signal.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models: semantic distance effect
finding: Humans and GPT-3 both do worse on four-term verbal analogies when the analog pairs are semantically distant.
numbers: Jones et al. dataset, 120 problems (40 per relation type: categorical, causal, compositional; half semantically near, half far). GPT-3 semantic-distance effect OR=3.24, p=0.0165.
limits: GPT-3 only. Direction of the odds ratio should be checked in the paper before quoting.
agent_relevance: A measured human-like cost of distance inside the model; relevant boundary for far sources.

source: Wenger and Kenett (2025): authors' implication
finding: Authors warn that any LLM as creative partner may push all users toward the same narrow set of 'creative' outputs, not just one model.
numbers: 22 LLMs tested; null of equal originality means, one-sided Welch tests at alpha 0.01.
limits: The warning is interpretation, not a tested effect on users.
agent_relevance: Argues against using a second LLM as the source of diversity; use an outside corpus.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024): creative writing extension
finding: On haiku, movie synopsis and flash fiction, top DAT models (GPT-3.5, Vicuna, GPT-4) were compared with human text by Divergent Semantic Integration and Lempel-Ziv complexity; LLMs approach but fall short of highly creative humans.
numbers: Abstract: LLMs 'approach human creative writing abilities' but 'fall short of the typical performance of highly creative humans'.
limits: DSI and LZ numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Semantic distance is cheap for models; sustained coherent far combination is not shown.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024): prompt format sensitivity
finding: Best GPT-4 prompt for letter-string analogies was Hodel and West's format (system line, fictional alphabet shown, worked pattern), so prompt format matters in analogy tests.
numbers: Results are in figures; no numbers extracted.
limits: Prompt sensitivity noted, not quantified here.
agent_relevance: Our mapping checks must fix the prompt format and test a second format.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?: retrieval step
finding: Baseline agent uses RAG with k=10 papers chosen at random from the top retrieved, titles and abstracts prepended. Retrieval is topical (near), not cross-domain.
numbers: k=10 papers; then dedupe at cosine 0.8 and rank.
limits: No test of distant retrieval in the paper.
agent_relevance: The gap our open-mode trial fills: far-domain retrieval in this pipeline judged by humans or by running is untested in opened sources.
